stories.title: A necroptotic-to-apoptotic signaling axis underlies inflammatory bowel disease
stories.authors_source: Jiyi Pang, Aysha H. Al-Ani, Komal M. Patel et al. — Science
stories.takeaway: Human IBD epithelium can retain a cell-death-primed state even during mild or clinically controlled disease, and stronger death signaling predicted later relapse.
stories.what_happened: Using about 900 biopsies from 80 people, patient-derived intestinal organoids and longitudinal follow-up, the study identifies a necroptotic-to-apoptotic signaling program that persists beyond overt inflammation.
stories.method: Human intestinal biopsies, patient-derived intestinal organoids, molecular cell-death profiling and >2-year clinical follow-up.
stories.why_it_matters: This strongly supports the idea that patient-derived IBD epithelium can carry intrinsic or durable pathological susceptibility even without an acute inflammatory trigger. That is directly aligned with interpreting baseline dysfunction in Crohn's-derived chips before microbiota exposure.
stories.read_first: Start with the patient-organoid experiments defining the necroptotic-to-apoptotic axis, then the analysis linking epithelial death signaling to subsequent relapse.
stories.caveat: The work identifies a predictive epithelial state but does not establish that this pathway alone initiates relapse; immune, stromal and microbiome inputs remain important upstream modifiers.

stories.title: Development of a gut-on-a-chip microfluidic device with three-dimensionally printed human intestinal tissue for studying human–microbe interactions
stories.authors_source: Lindy K. Jang et al. — Biofabrication / Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
stories.takeaway: A microscope-slide-sized gut chip uses stereolithographically printed GelMA-based crypt–villus architecture, a removable tissue gasket and temporal sampling to study human–microbe interactions in a structurally controlled intestinal model.
stories.what_happened: The team printed intestinal topography, improved scaffold cell compatibility through protein crosslinking, seeded human intestinal cells off-chip and integrated the tissue into a two-sided fluidic device with repeated sampling and microbiome-prediction workflows.
stories.method: SLA 3D printing, GelMA bioresins, protein surface functionalization, modular microfluidics, human intestinal culture and longitudinal sampling.
stories.why_it_matters: This is unusually close to your engineering interests: it treats intestinal geometry and chip assembly as reproducible manufactured components rather than relying entirely on spontaneous morphogenesis. The removable gasket is also worth comparing with your own modular alignment and multiplexing concepts.
stories.read_first: Read the chip architecture and fabrication figure first, then the validation of crypt–villus tissue behavior and temporal sampling strategy.
stories.caveat: Printed geometry improves reproducibility but can impose architecture rather than reproduce self-organized tissue mechanics; the biological fidelity of the scaffold must therefore be judged independently from its geometric resemblance.

stories.title: PPARδ-Hmgcs2 Ketone Body Signaling Mediates Intestinal Stem Cells Regeneration After IR Exposure
stories.authors_source: Yuhan Gan, Yu Gao, Liao Zhang et al. — Cell Transplantation
stories.takeaway: PPARδ-Hmgcs2-linked ketone-body signaling promotes intestinal stem-cell regeneration after ionizing-radiation injury, connecting metabolic state directly to epithelial recovery.
stories.what_happened: The study used 9.5-Gy total-body irradiation in mice and pharmacologic PPARδ activation to interrogate intestinal stem-cell regeneration and the downstream Hmgcs2/ketogenesis program.
stories.method: Mouse radiation injury, 60Co irradiation, PPARδ agonism, intestinal stem-cell/regeneration assays and metabolic-pathway analysis.
stories.why_it_matters: For your radiation-on-chip work, this provides a candidate recovery axis downstream of injury rather than another generic antioxidant mechanism. HMGCS2/ketone biology could help distinguish metabolic regeneration from simple ROS suppression.
stories.read_first: Read the experiments linking PPARδ activation to Hmgcs2 and ISC regeneration, then examine whether protection reflects preserved stemness, increased proliferation or altered survival.
stories.caveat: The model is high-dose whole-body irradiation in mice; whether the same metabolic program dominates in differentiated human Caco-2 or patient-derived intestinal epithelium is unresolved.

stories.title: Harnessing microfluidics for microbiology: from bacteria-host interactions to emerging cancer therapies
stories.authors_source: Léa Pinon, Auriane Debache, Alexandre Thuaud et al. — Communications Biology
stories.takeaway: Microfluidics is increasingly valuable not merely for culturing bacteria but for resolving colonization dynamics, environmental control and host–bacteria interactions with temporal and spatial precision.
stories.what_happened: The review connects foundational bacterial single-cell microfluidics with organ-on-chip host–microbe systems and argues for controlled physicochemical niches as a prerequisite for mechanistic microbiology.
stories.method: Review of microfluidic microbiology, live imaging, bacterial population dynamics and host–microbe organ-on-chip approaches.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a useful design paper for your microbiota-chip work because it emphasizes that oxygen, nutrients, shear and spatial confinement are experimental variables rather than background conditions. Those variables can select which organisms persist and therefore change the epithelial phenotype.
stories.read_first: Start with the host–bacteria organ-on-chip section and figures comparing microfluidic control of microbial niches and colonization dynamics.
stories.caveat: Much of the review spans non-intestinal and cancer applications, so its engineering principles transfer more directly than its biological conclusions.

stories.title: FDA direct final rule modernizing nonclinical testing terminology to explicitly encompass NAMs
stories.authors_source: U.S. Food and Drug Administration / Federal Register
stories.takeaway: FDA regulatory language now explicitly frames cell-based assays, organ chips, microphysiological systems, computer modeling and bioprinting as nonclinical approaches alongside animal studies rather than defining animal testing as the default category.
stories.what_happened: The September 22 direct final rule updates drug and biologics regulations across 21 CFR Parts 312, 314, 315, 361 and 601; FDA also surfaced NAM use-case examples from prior reviews.
stories.method: Federal regulatory rulemaking and codification of nonclinical-test terminology following FDORA.
stories.why_it_matters: This is strategically important for how you frame organ-chip work: the regulatory question is increasingly context-of-use and evidentiary fitness, not whether an assay is 'alternative' to an animal model. That language is useful for future grants, papers and job positioning around NAM translation.
stories.read_first: Read the definitions of nonclinical test/study and the IND-related sections that explicitly recognize organ chips and computational methods, then inspect FDA's NAM use-case database.
stories.caveat: The rule changes terminology and formal recognition; it does not mean every organ-chip assay is validated, qualified or accepted for a specific regulatory decision.

stories.title: Smart organoid-on-chip systems: From microfluidics to sensors, control, and AI
stories.authors_source: Hina Wajid and Sumreen Begum — The International Journal of Artificial Organs
stories.takeaway: The next useful step for organoid-on-chip platforms is closed-loop measurement and control: sensors, microcontroller-based actuation and computational interpretation can convert descriptive culture systems into quantitative experimental platforms.
stories.what_happened: The review synthesizes sensor-integrated microfluidics, environmental control and AI-based analysis for organoid-on-chip systems, emphasizing reproducibility and longitudinal monitoring.
stories.method: Review of organoid-on-chip microfluidics, sensors, automation, control systems and AI-driven analysis.
stories.why_it_matters: This maps directly onto your multiplexing work. Equal flow is only one control problem; a more mature platform would measure outputs such as pressure, barrier function or chemistry and use them to detect or correct channel-to-channel drift.
stories.read_first: Read the sensor/control architecture sections first and identify which variables are measured continuously versus inferred computationally.
stories.caveat: The field often labels systems 'smart' before demonstrating robust closed-loop control; distinguish genuine feedback control from passive sensing plus post hoc AI analysis.

stories.title: Nanoplasmonic Aptasensing Enables Real-Time Optical Monitoring of Neurotransmitters in Living Brainstem Organoids
stories.authors_source: Hanjun Cho et al. — ACS Nano
stories.takeaway: A microfluidic organoid-on-chip couples a nanoplasmonic aptamer sensor to living organoids for non-destructive, real-time secretome monitoring and time-resolved drug-response measurement.
stories.what_happened: The platform detects dopamine at picomolar sensitivity from brainstem organoids and follows L-DOPA response continuously over 12 hours without destructive sampling.
stories.method: Stem-cell-derived organoids, microfluidics, gold nanohole optical cavities, aptamer sensing and longitudinal pharmacodynamic measurements.
stories.why_it_matters: Different organ, but the measurement concept is excellent for gut chips: continuous extracellular sensing could capture ROS, metabolites or barrier-associated signals that endpoint imaging misses and could eventually provide feedback signals for multiplex control.
stories.read_first: Start with the sensor–chip integration figure, then the 12-hour L-DOPA response curves showing onset, peak and duration.
stories.caveat: Dopamine is a comparatively sensor-friendly defined analyte; translating this to complex gut-chip media and reactive species will face specificity, fouling and calibration problems.

stories.title: Microbiome-host communication via vaccenic acid modulates LRH-1/NR5A2 activity and ameliorates metabolic liver disease
stories.authors_source: Anna Pia Plazzo et al. — EMBO Molecular Medicine
stories.takeaway: Vaccenic acid provides a defined microbial/dietary metabolite-to-host receptor mechanism, activating LRH-1/NR5A2 and improving inflammatory and metabolic phenotypes in vivo.
stories.what_happened: The authors identified vaccenic acid as a ligand for LRH-1/NR5A2 and linked receptor activation to reduced blood glucose, lipids and fatty-liver phenotypes in mice.
stories.method: Ligand discovery, receptor biology, bacterial/metabolite analysis and mouse metabolic-disease experiments.
stories.why_it_matters: For your FMT work, the useful lesson is methodological: move from community-level protection to a defined metabolite → host receptor → phenotype chain. That is the level of mechanism that can turn an FMT observation into a tractable epithelial hypothesis.
stories.read_first: Read the ligand-identification experiments first, then the receptor-dependence and in-vivo rescue data.
stories.caveat: The primary disease phenotype is metabolic liver disease rather than intestinal inflammation, and dietary exposure contributes to vaccenic-acid availability, complicating attribution solely to gut microbial production.

stories.title: Early-life gut microbiome maturation trajectories are associated with islet autoimmunity and type 1 diabetes risk
stories.takeaway: Longitudinal microbiome maturation trajectories, rather than a single compositional snapshot, stratified later autoimmune risk; an early-plateaued trajectory carried roughly threefold higher risk in a high-risk pediatric cohort.
stories.what_happened: More than 12,000 stool samples from 887 children were used to define microbiome-development trajectories across the first six years of life and relate them to islet autoimmunity/type 1 diabetes outcomes and host genetics.
stories.method: Longitudinal pediatric cohort, repeated stool microbiome profiling, trajectory modeling and host-genetic interaction analysis.
stories.why_it_matters: Although not IBD, this reinforces an important principle for microbiota experiments: community state is history-dependent. A donor sample is a snapshot of an ecological trajectory, which may partly explain why taxonomically similar donor communities produce different functional phenotypes.
stories.read_first: Start with the trajectory definitions and risk curves, then the host-genotype interaction analysis.
stories.caveat: This is observational and disease-specific; maturation trajectories associated with autoimmune diabetes cannot be assumed to generalize directly to adult FMT or Crohn's disease.

stories.title: B cells drive and predict immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated colitis
stories.authors_source: Naimah Turner, Synat Keam, Noha Abdel-Wahab et al. — Cell Reports / MD Anderson
stories.takeaway: Elevated B-cell activity preceded immune-checkpoint-inhibitor colitis, while B-cell blockade reduced disease in preclinical models, identifying an adaptive-immune driver rather than treating epithelial injury as the whole mechanism.
stories.what_happened: The study linked circulating B-cell features to later colitis and used mechanistic preclinical experiments to test whether B-cell depletion alters disease severity.
stories.method: Human immunotherapy cohorts, immune profiling and preclinical colitis models with B-cell perturbation.
stories.why_it_matters: This is not classical IBD, but it is a useful counterpoint for epithelial models: similar colitis phenotypes can arise from very different upstream immune mechanisms. It helps define what an epithelial-only Crohn's chip can and cannot claim mechanistically.
stories.read_first: Read the pre-symptomatic B-cell association first, then the B-cell-blockade experiment establishing functional contribution.
stories.caveat: Checkpoint-inhibitor colitis has a distinct initiating mechanism from Crohn's disease, so shared downstream pathology should not be mistaken for shared etiology.
